skin-whitening-bleaching.text: Users apply or take lightening agents to fade dark spots and lift overall skin tone, and some forum posters say it raises their rating by about 0.5 to 1 PSL. Topical agents such as hydroquinone and arbutin have clinical study for pigmentation; the rating claim rests on anecdote.

pheromone-cologne.text: Buyers wear these scents hoping the added pheromones make them more attractive to others, as a fragrance-based add-on to grooming and presentation. The attraction effect is based on marketing and anecdote, and reviewers report no human pheromone shown to change behavior.

frenotomy-tongue-tie-release-for-face.text: Forum posters discuss releasing the tongue frenulum so the tongue can rest against the palate, in the hope of a more defined jaw, better profile and straighter teeth. Studies cover feeding and speech outcomes; the facial-appearance link is untested and rests on anecdote.

face-rating-apps-ai-scoring.text: Users submit photos to apps and AI tools to get an attractiveness number or tier, then track it across haircuts, grooming changes or angles, and some convert it to PSL. The scores are model outputs, and accuracy as a guide to real-world appeal is largely unstudied.

psl-scale.text: Community members use the PSL scale as a shared yardstick to rate male faces and to measure progress from changes such as skin, hair or leanness. It is an informal forum system, not scientifically validated, and ratings reflect community opinion.

chain: Eyes read as sharper, more alert
canthal-tilt-theory.text: Forum users measure the angle of the eye corners and treat a positive tilt as a marker of attractiveness, with some suggesting posture, mewing or surgery to change it. The tilt itself is measurable; the strong rule built on it and the non-surgical change claims are poorly studied.

hunter-eyes.text: Hunter eyes are described online as an ideal eye area, with a positive tilt, deep set and low brows, and some users try squinting or exercises to approximate it. There is no formal medical definition and little direct research on attractiveness or on trainability.

facial-width-to-height-ratio-fwhr.text: Forum users calculate fWHR from photos and treat a higher ratio as a sign of masculinity and attractiveness, then weigh beards, hairstyles or procedures against it. Research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression; the attractiveness use is largely untested.

golden-ratio-face-analysis.text: Forum posters measure features such as eye spacing and mouth-to-nose width against phi (about 1.618) and other ideal ratios to decide what to change. Research has found little support for phi as a driver of attractiveness, and the precision of the scores is unvalidated.

mogging-amog.text: Looksmaxxers use mogging as slang for outshining another man in a given setting, and it frames goals such as height, jaw or style improvements. It is a social concept based on anecdote, with no research of its own.

black-pill-ideology.text: The black pill is a belief from incel communities that genetics and looks largely fix a man's outcomes, and looksmaxxing forums discuss it as the pessimistic counterpart to improvement-focused approaches. Researchers have studied it mainly for links to mental-health burden and misogynistic extremism, not for effects on appearance.

halo-effect.text: Looksmaxxers cite the halo effect as the reason appearance gains pay off beyond looks, shaping how competent, likable and trustworthy others perceive them. The effect is well documented in psychology; community claims about its size across school, work and dating vary.

chain: Looks form part of overall desirability
Changes to face and body shift it
sexual-market-value-smv.text: Manosphere and looksmaxxing users treat SMV as a total desirability score and use it to prioritise changes such as skin, hair, fitness and style. It is a community term loosely related to academic mate value research, and the community's specific weightings are untested.

jestermaxxing.text: Forum users describe leaning on humor and clowning to win social and romantic interest, as a complement to looks. Research exists on humor and attraction generally, but the term and its claims about less attractive men are based on anecdote.

looksmatching.text: Forum users use looksmatching to describe couples rated at a similar attractiveness level and to calibrate who they can expect to attract after improving. It parallels the psychology matching hypothesis, which has real but mixed support.

chain: Fuller-looking hair or a planned cut
norwood-scale.text: Users place their hairline on the seven-stage Norwood chart to size up male pattern hair loss and choose among treatments, transplants, hair systems or a buzz cut. The scale is a standard clinical classification used by dermatologists and hair restoration surgeons.

chain: Left and right sides match more closely
facial-symmetry-theory.text: Looksmaxxers use symmetry as a guide for what to correct first, trying fillers, implants, posture work or bone-related methods to even out the face. Studies find a real but modest link between symmetry and attractiveness; changing asymmetry through posture or non-surgical methods is untested.

dimorphism-theory.text: Forum users treat masculine features such as a strong jaw and defined cheekbones as central to male attractiveness, and use the idea to choose beards, fat loss or procedures. Research on facial masculinity and attractiveness is real but mixed.

ascension.text: Ascension is the community word for a big improvement in looks over time, and forum threads document plans and progress with before-and-after photos. It names an outcome rather than a method, and results shown are individual self-reports.

hairstyle-maxxing.text: Users pick a cut and styling to suit face shape, forehead size and hair type, and the change is visible as soon as the haircut is done. Research shows hair shapes first impressions, though how much it adds beyond the underlying face is debated.

color-analysis.text: Users have their skin tone, hair and eyes assigned to a season, then wear clothing and makeup in that palette so colors near the face flatter them. The visible effect of a color is immediate; little rigorous research backs the specific four-season categories.

voice-maxxing.text: Users practise pitch, resonance and delivery techniques, borrowed from speech therapy, to sound deeper or more masculine and come across as more attractive. Speech-therapy methods exist for voice change; no trials test them for attractiveness.

dripmaxxing-fashion.text: Users improve clothing, fit, accessories and styling to look better without changing the face or body, and the difference shows as soon as they are dressed. It is a low-cost approach discussed in forums, with no clinical research behind it.

beard-maxxing.text: Users grow and shape a beard to frame the jaw, disguise a recessed chin or add masculinity, and the change is visible as the beard fills in. Minoxidil or transplants are sometimes discussed for patchy growth. Research on beards and attractiveness is mixed.

squintmaxxing.text: Proponents narrow the eyelids slightly, in photos and in daily habit, to get the intense look called hunter eyes. It is a free, instant adjustment, though its effect on ratings and attractiveness is untested and based on anecdote.

dental-work-teeth-maxxing.text: Users whiten teeth with strips, pastes and dentist treatments, often alongside orthodontics, for a brighter and neater smile. Peroxide whitening products have clinical trial support, and the shade change is visible after use.

hair-dye-bleaching-hair.text: Users dye or bleach scalp hair, eyebrows, lashes or facial hair to change contrast, cover grey, or make sparse brows and beards look darker and fuller. The colour change is visible straight after application and is a common cosmetic practice.

chain: Carotenoids build up in outer skin
carrot-maxxing.text: Users eat large amounts of carrots and other carotenoid-rich foods to give the skin a golden glow without sun exposure. Carotenemia is a documented, benign condition, and the tint builds up over weeks.

tyrosine-supplements-for-tanning.text: Users take tyrosine pills or apply lotions on the theory that more of melanin's building block means a faster or deeper tan. Tyrosine's role in melanin is established biology; human trials of it for tanning have not been done.

baby-oil-tanning.text: Users apply baby oil before sun exposure in the belief it speeds or deepens a tan, a habit dating to the mid-twentieth century. The oils typically contain no sunscreen filter, and there are no studies behind the claimed tanning benefit.
